1.2. Project Overview  
730 Stanyan is an eight-story 160-unit mixed-use affordable rental housing 
development serving TAY, Adults and Family households with 1 manager’s unit, 
32 units set aside as Section 8 Project-Based Voucher (PBV) Units, 20 PSH units 
for TAY, 12 PSH units for Families, and 95 general affordable (lottery) units.  
Twelve of the 20 PSH TAY units and seven of the 12 PSH Family units are also 
supported by No Place Like Home (NPLH) capital (building construction) 
funding and are intended for residents with higher acuity levels of 
behavioral/mental health challenges. Ten TAY units are studios, and ten units are 
one-bedroom units-that will typically serve parenting youth and young adults.  
TNDC and CCDC were selected to co-develop affordable rental housing at 730 
Stanyan, based on a proposal submitted in response to a 730 Stanyan Request for 
Qualifications, issued by MOHCD on September 10, 2019.    
Construction at 730 Stanyan began in June 2023, and the Sponsors expect to 
receive a temporary certificate of occupancy (TCO) and begin lease-up in August 
2025. The Project is an eight-story concrete building with seven floors of 
residential units encompassing 35 studios, 43 one-bedrooms, 42 two-bedrooms, 
and 40 three-bedrooms. The residential entry is situated along Stanyan Street, 
and the ground floor includes four commercial spaces, accessed on all three 
building frontages (Haight Street, Stanyan Street and Waller Street), including: a 
Felton-operated neighborhood serving early childhood education center (ECEC) 
accessed from Waller Street and a space intended for a cafe/restaurant at the 
corner of Stanyan and Haight streets. In addition, spaces for two non-profit or 
retail tenants are contemplated for the remaining commercial spaces along 
Haight Street and at the corner of Waller and Stanyan streets. The ground floor 
will also include common areas for residents of the building, including a lobby, 
community room, bike storage room, common restrooms, kitchen (within the

The Project operating budget is primarily supported by LOSP, tenant paid rents,

with its asset management team and confirmed it with HSH. Income from tenant 
paid rents are escalated 1% annually for the PSH and PBV units and are 
escalated 2.5% annually for general affordable units annually.   
 
The LOSP contract covers the difference between the cost to operate the property 
and tenant rent payments. For the first year, this LOSP contract is estimated at 
$568,307, and pro-rated based on five months of operations in 2025.

Attachment A: LOSP Program Description 
 
 
As part of the City and County of San Francisco’s effort to address the needs of the growing 
homeless population, the City has prioritized the development of non-profit owned and operated 
permanent supportive housing for formerly homeless individuals and families. While capital 
financing can be leveraged for this population, stakeholders realized these units cannot be 
feasibly operated at the scale needed if they rely solely on scarce federal or state operating 
subsidies.  
 
In June 2004, the City launched its Ten Year Plan to Abolish Chronic Homelessness (the 2004 
10-Year Plan), a multifaceted approach that included a locally funded operating subsidy as a key 
element and established the Local Operating Subsidy Program (LOSP) in 2006 to support the 
creation of permanent supportive housing at a large scale. The operating subsidy leverages capital 
financing by integrating homeless units into Low Income Housing Tax Credit projects without 
burdening them with operating deficits. LOSP was created by the Mayor’s Office of Housing and 
Community Development (MOHCD) in partnership with the Department of Public Health (DPH) 
and the Human Services Agency (HSA).  
 
On July 1, 2016, the City’s diverse programs addressing homelessness were brought under the 
new Department of Homelessness and Supportive Housing (HSH), which combines key 
homeless-serving programs and contracts previously located across several City departments. The 
new department consolidates the functions of DPH Direct Access to Housing (DAH) and HSA 
Housing & Homeless programs. San Francisco is developing a Coordinated Entry System (CES) 
for all homeless populations to best match households to the appropriate intervention and ensure 
those with the highest needs are prioritized.  
 
Through grant agreements with MOHCD, which are subject to annual appropriations by the 
Board of Supervisors, LOSP pays the difference between the cost of operating housing for 
homeless persons and all other sources of operating revenue for a given project, such as tenant 
rental payments, commercial space lease payments, or other operating subsidies. HSH refers 
homeless applicants to the housing units as well as provides services funding to the projects under 
a separate contract.
